title: Ethereum whale's $13.45M loss reflects a year-long exit, not a fresh ETH dump
body: Ethereum whale's $13.45 million loss is a year-long exit, not a fresh dump A wallet that began buying Ethereum (ETH) near last year's market peak has now moved almost its entire position onto exchanges. On-chain analyst Ai Yi flagged the activity, Odaily reported it, and Binance News carried it on Friday. The headline figure, a potential $13.45 million loss on 15,361 ETH, checks out arithmetically. But it describes twelve months of activity, not a single sale this week, and that difference matters for how traders should read it. What the wallet actually did The investor started buying in September 2025 at around $4,600 and kept adding as prices fell. In total, 15,810 ETH was withdrawn from exchanges at an average cost of about $4,100, roughly $65 million. Between October 2025 and October 2026, the wallet sent 15,361 ETH back to exchanges at an average price of about $3,226. The most recent deposit came a few hours before the report, but its size was not disclosed. The wallet still holds 572 ETH. Why a deposit is not the same as a sale Moving coins onto an exchange often comes before selling, which is why analysts track these transfers. But on-chain data shows that coins moved, not that they were sold. Exchange deposits can also be used as collateral for borrowing or for internal transfers. The $13.45 million figure is therefore an estimate. It assumes every deposited coin was sold at the market price on the day it arrived.

title: PBOC is expected to set the USD/CNY reference rate at 6.6947 – Reuters estimate
body: The fixing mechanism matters most right now because its message has shifted over the past month. For nearly a year, the PBOC has set its daily guidance weaker than market expectations, which traders read as an effort to slow the yuan's appreciation, and in late August that gap reached its widest since February, shortly after the yuan touched a three-and-a-half-year high. Through September, however, the midpoint has strengthened at a faster pace, narrowing its gap with market expectations and suggesting the central bank has eased its resistance to yuan gains. The fixing is still set weaker than models imply, so this looks like a loosening of the brakes rather than their removal. The balance Beijing is weighing is unchanged: a firmer currency supports capital stability and import costs, but too rapid a rise risks eroding export competitiveness while the domestic economy remains soft. The rejection this week at 5.30% following the US CPI report stands out rather clearly, with yields failing to sustain a break higher before retreating sharply. And that now puts the spotlight back on the 5.00% level, which had previously played the role in keeping yields from breaking out back in September. title: Felix Nikolas Prehn on mortgage rates and the 10-year Treasury yield
body: Felix Nikolas Prehn is an economist and former investment banker whose research examines money, asset prices and US households from 2000 to 2026. A buyer who opens a mortgage quote is looking at the last link in a chain that starts in the bond market. The starting point for a mortgage rate A St. Louis Fed explainer on mortgage rates names the 10-year Treasury note as the benchmark for the 30-year mortgage. Treasury securities count as very low risk because the US government backs them, so investors use their yields as the yardstick for other long-term investments. The choice of a 10-year note for a 30-year loan comes down to how long people keep their mortgages. Many are written for 30 years, but most are paid off, refinanced or ended by the sale of the home well before then. The average life of a mortgage is much closer to 10 years. Some banks bundle thousands of mortgages into securities and sell them to investors, who receive the principal and interest homeowners pay. Those investors compare the return on mortgage-backed securities with the return on the 10-year note. The two respond to the same signals, such as data on inflation and economic growth, and their yields often move in the same direction. The securities are riskier than Treasuries, so investors demand a higher yield for taking that risk. The explainer calls the market value of that extra risk, plus the added costs of a mortgage (origination expenses, servicing fees and lender profit), the mortgage spread.

title: Where do traders get interest rate expectations for central banks?
body: Interest rate expectations are among the most important drivers for financial markets. They influence government bond yields, currencies, equity valuations, and even cryptocurrencies. But how can traders check whether the market expects a central bank to cut rates, hold them steady, or deliver rate hikes? The answer lies in interest rate derivatives, particularly overnight index swaps (OIS) and interest rate futures. These instruments allow market participants to express views on future interest rates, hedge their exposure to changes in monetary policy, and translate market prices into implied expectations. The market doesn't wait for a central bank meeting to form expectations about its next decision. Traders can buy and sell derivatives whose value depends on interest rates over specific future periods. When macro or geopolitical developments change the future outlook, or central bank officials communication hints to a certain decision, traders reassess the likely path of monetary policy before the central bank takes action. They then adjust their positions in interest rate derivatives, causing prices to move. These price movements can be translated into implied interest rates. By comparing the implied rate with the current policy rate, traders can estimate how much tightening or easing the market has priced in. There are two main instruments for this purpose: overnight index swaps and interest rate futures.

title: Germany 10-Year Bund Yield Holds Near 5-Week Low
body: The German 10-year Bund yield was little changed at around 3.42%, hovering near a five-week low, and was down nearly 7 bps for the week. The move tracked a global decline in borrowing costs as expectations for further monetary policy tightening eased. Remarks by Fed Chair Warsh at the IMF summit were widely interpreted as signaling that the Federal Reserve is likely to keep rates unchanged this month, despite inflation data coming in hotter than expected. In Europe, comments from ECB President Lagarde supported a cautious, wait-and-see stance. Lagarde noted that elevated inflation in the Eurozone has been driven "predominantly, but not exclusively" by a surge in energy prices following the Iran war. title: US September import price index +1.1% vs +0.8% expected
body: Prior was +0.7% m/m (revised to +0.5%) Export prices +2.2% vs +1.0% expected Prior export prices were +0.6% (revised to +1.2%) Import prices y/y 8.1% vs +7.0% prior It's been an ugly week for inflation data. The market seems to think the Fed can tame it by waiting until December but that's some serious imported inflation that's going to be working its way through prices for awhile. The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes the import and export price indexes monthly. They measure what US buyers pay for foreign goods and services and what foreign buyers pay for American output. The data rarely moves markets on its own, but it is a useful read on how the dollar, global commodity prices and foreign producer costs are feeding into the US economy. One point worth knowing: import prices exclude tariffs and duties. That makes the series a clean test of whether foreign exporters are absorbing tariff costs or passing them through. It is also one of the inputs used to deflate trade in the GDP accounts. In August, import prices rose 0.7%, and energy dominated. Import fuel prices were up 26.8% from a year earlier, and natural gas import prices more than doubled, rising 102.6%. Export prices climbed 8.6% over the 12 months to August. China stands out: import prices from China rose 1.0% in August, the biggest monthly gain since the series started in January 2004. The September report follows two hot inflation prints this week.

title: Eurozone September final CPI +3.8% vs +3.8% y/y prelim
body: Eurozone September final CPI +3.8% vs +3.8% y/y prelim Prior +3.2% Eurozone September final core CPI +2.5% vs +2.5% y/y prelim Prior +2.4% There are no changes to the preliminary estimates, with euro area headline inflation confirmed to have surged to 3.8% in September. That marks a notable acceleration from the 3.2% estimate in August, with energy price inflation being the main culprit. Of note, energy prices were up 4.0% monthly and 18.9% annually in September (as compared to 14.3% annually in August). While the ECB may be able to look past the acceleration in headline prices, it will be tough for policymakers to keep brushing aside further increases in core inflation. The annual estimate here is seen rising to 2.5% from 2.4% previously. And that owes much to a further increase in services inflation, up to 3.2% in September from 3.0% in August. The final report here continues to reaffirm the narrative that the ECB cannot rest on its laurels as we look towards the final stretch of the year. Inflation pressures are heating up and with economic conditions as well as fiscal risks intensifying, policymakers will have a rather challenging task in trying to balance all of that heading into next year. title: Flying car. Grounded stock. The technicals are not leaning to a "take-off" for Tesla stock
body: The flying car gets attention. But is it good for business? Tesla's flying car has certainly brought out the "oohs" and "aahs." And why not? A car that can briefly take flight is going to get attention. From a marketing perspective, that is a win for Tesla. It gets people talking and gives Elon Musk another opportunity to show what his engineers can do. But is it good for the business? That is where I have some questions. How many people need a flying sports car? How much will it cost to develop and produce? Could that money—and engineering talent—be better spent on vehicles that more people can afford and use every day? Will the flying version ever get approved for public use? Or is it simply a gimmick? I am still waiting for the flux capacitor and the time-machine capability. Nevertheless, the publicity has value. The payoff for shareholders is less clear. Elon had his moment. Now the market gets its turn. Which brings me to the technicals. Despite all the excitement, the price action helps tell us whether the market is buying the idea—or selling it. And Tesla's technical picture is not overly bullish. The car got off the ground. Can the stock do the same? Let's look at the levels. Elon Musk had his moment yesterday. Today, the market gets its turn. At the open, Tesla shares moved higher, reaching $370.58. However, that high fell just short of the 100-day moving average at $371.13. Buyers had their shot to test that key technical target. They could not get above it.

title: Baltic Dry Index at Over 3-Month Low
body: The Baltic Exchange's dry bulk freight index, which measures shipping rates for vessels transporting dry bulk commodities, fell about 1.3% on Friday to 2,515 points, its lowest level since June 30 and its tenth consecutive daily decline. Persistent weak iron ore demand and subdued sentiment in China's steel market continued to pressure Capesize rates, while ample vessel availability further weighed on the market. The Capesize index — reflecting earnings for vessels that typically carry 150,000-ton cargoes such as iron ore and coal — slid 2.2% to 3,249 points, its lowest reading since early April. The Panamax index, which covers ships that usually transport 60,000–70,000 tons of coal or grain, fell 1.8% to 2,314 points. Among smaller segments, the Supramax index rose 0.5% to 1,865 points. Overall, the benchmark Baltic Dry Index declined about 14% over the week, extending its losing streak to a third consecutive week. title: Oil prices surge higher into the weekend
body: It will be another weekend of pain at the fuel pumps. WTI crude oil is finishing the week at the highest since September 21 and back over $100 per barrel. WTI last trade up $3.33 to $101.30. Brent crude also touched $110 for the first time since May. The strong rally to $101 from $98 in the final hours of trading today suggsets lingering worries about US attacks on Iran, particularly after all the news floated this week about the US military preparing MOAB attacks. Trump himself didn't push back against the reports when given the opportunity but he also previously wrote that the US won't attack Iran before the midterms. At the same time, things aren't looking great for Republicans in the polls and today the White House announced that new press secretary Katie Zacharia was asked to step down after just five days. We also learned today the US 2026 fiscal year deficit was the highest in five years. Trump may see fresh attacks as a Hail Mary opportunity to try to change the narrative around the war and inflation. Alternatively, Iran could try to escalate in order to further drive up oil prices and exact a toll on global consumers in order to gain leverage. In any case, there is no real catalyst in the news for today's big gain in oil. What it's doing is reverberating back into stock and bond markets and driving one of the worst days of the year in the Nasdaq, which was last down 2.2%.

title: US fiscal 2026 budget deficit was the largest in five years
body: September 2025 was a $198B surplus Outlays $585B vs $346B a year ago Receipts $558B vs $544B a year ago FY2026 deficit $1.992 trillion vs $1.775T in FY2025, the largest in five years FY2026 gross interest on the debt: record $1.36T, up $144B (12%) Interest is now the main driver of the deficit. The $144B rise in interest costs accounts for about two-thirds of the $217B increase in the full-year shortfall. Treasury will keep rolling debt at higher rates while the Fed is debating hikes rather than cuts, so that line has nowhere to go but up. The customs numbers are the most interesting part of the release. Gross customs receipts were $25.27B, roughly in line with the recent run rate. But refunds of $19.36B ate up 77% of that, leaving net customs receipts of just $5.91B. The monthly swing from a $198B surplus to a $27B deficit is mostly about outlays, which jumped $239B y/y while receipts rose only 2.6%. Year-ago September comparisons are notoriously noisy because of payment timing, so the full-year number is the one that matters. In any case, the headline tells most of the story as the US is in a huge fiscal hole and these are the good times for growth right now. There are going to be some very ugly days ahead and there's no way to grow out of it. This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.
